mainTopic: Why the rule of מודה במקצת (partial admission requires a שבועה) applies to a loan (מלוה) and not to a deposit (פקדון), using רבה's explanation that a borrower will not brazenly lie to his lender's face.
overview: The amud opens by answering a difficulty from the previous amud. The words 'כי הוא זה', which teach that one who admits part of a claim must swear, appear among the laws of deposits. The גמרא says this is עירוב פרשיות: the words really refer to a loan. It then asks why a loan is different and answers with רבה's famous reasoning. A borrower would like to deny the whole debt, but he is too embarrassed to lie to the face of the person who lent him money. He would also like to admit everything, but he cannot pay right now, so he stalls by denying part. The Torah puts a שבועה on him to push him to admit all of it. That reasoning fits only a loan. With a פקדון the owner did no favor, so a person will lie to his face (מעיז ומעיז). At the very end, רמי בר חמא begins quoting a ברייתא about the four kinds of שומרים, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse about partial admission really refers to a loan
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the Torah's portions are mixed here: 'כי הוא זה' is written next to deposits, but it really refers to a loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah mixed two topics together here. The words 'this is it' are really talking about a loan.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves a difficulty from just before. The rule of partial admission comes from a פסוק in the deposit section, so how can it be limited to loans? It answers that this פסוק actually belongs to the topic of loans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'כי הוא זה' are the source for the rule that someone who admits part of a claim must swear. Even though they appear among the laws of a שומר, the גמרא says they were placed there as עירוב פרשיות and really refer to a מלוה. So the partial-admission rule is tied to loans.

keyTerms.meaning: A mixing of Torah sections: a law written in one section that really belongs to another
'This is it': the words that teach the oath for a partial admission

phrases.english: A mixing of Torah sections is written here,
and when it is written: "This is it,"
it is written about a loan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a difficulty raised on the previous amud: the partial-admission פסוק 'כי הוא זה' appears in the deposit section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the verse to a different topic (עירוב פרשיות)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since 'כי הוא זה' appears among the deposit laws, the partial-admission rule should apply to deposits.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse really refers to a loan, so the partial-admission rule belongs to loans.

steps.title: Why should a loan be different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what is special about a loan that the partial-admission rule applies only there.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different about a loan?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question that sets up the next move. It wants the reason the rule fits a loan specifically.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying that the verse refers to a loan is a reading of the text. The גמרא now wants the logic behind it: why would the Torah treat a borrower who admits part of a debt differently from a שומר who admits part of a deposit?

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? Asks for the distinction between two cases

phrases.english: And what is different about a loan?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the answer in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The logical reason the partial-admission oath applies specifically to a loan.

steps.title: רבה: a borrower won't deny everything to his lender's face
steps.stepSummary: The answer follows רבה. A borrower really wants to deny the whole debt, but he does not, because a person won't brazenly lie to the face of the one who lent to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It follows רבה, who said: Why did the Torah say that one who admits part of a claim must swear? Because we assume a person will not be brazen to the face of his creditor. This borrower really wants to deny the whole debt. He doesn't deny all of it only because a person won't be that brazen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting רבה's explanation of why the Torah requires a שבועה for a partial admission. This step gives the first half of the reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a חזקה that a borrower is too embarrassed to look his lender in the eye and lie completely. So when he admits part of the debt, it is not because he is honest. The embarrassment simply stops him from denying everything.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits part of the claim
A presumption about how people usually behave
His creditor, the one he owes money to

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the classic source for the חזקה 'אין אדם מעיז פניו בפני בעל חובו', which is used across ש״ס.

phrases.english: It is like Rabba, as Rabba said:
For what reason did the Torah say:
one who admits to part of the claim must swear?
There is a presumption that a person does not act brazenly
in front of his creditor;
and this man wants to deny all of it,
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is the corrected wording, so read it as 'all of it.'

phrases.english: and the fact that he does not deny it
is because a person does not act brazenly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2 by quoting רבה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A borrower is too embarrassed to deny everything to his lender's face. That is why he admits part.

steps.title: Why he denies part, and why the Torah adds a שבועה
steps.stepSummary: רבה continues. The borrower would like to admit everything but cannot pay now, so he denies part to stall. The Torah puts a שבועה on him to push him to admit the whole debt.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would really like to admit all of it. He denies part because he thinks: 'If I admit all of it, he will demand all of it from me now. Let me put him off for now until I have money, and then I'll pay.' So the Torah puts an oath on him, to get him to admit all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה finishes his explanation. He says why the borrower denies part of the debt, and why the Torah answers this with a שבועה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The partial denial is not a plan to steal. It is a stalling tactic by someone short on cash. Since he is not a hardened liar, the threat of a שבועה is likely to make him admit the whole debt. רחמנא imposes the oath for exactly that purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: I will slip away from him or put him off
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳

phrases.english: And he wants to admit to him about all of it,
and the fact that he denies part to him
is because he thinks: If I admit all of it to him,
he will demand all of it from me;
let me at least put him off now
until I have money, and then I will pay.
Therefore the Merciful One put an oath on him,
so that he will admit all of it to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבה's explanation that began in step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He denies part only to stall. The Torah imposes a שבועה to push him to admit everything.

steps.title: This reasoning works only for a loan, not a deposit
steps.stepSummary: רבה's reasoning applies only to a loan. With a deposit, a person will act brazenly without hesitation, so the special partial-admission logic does not fit.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is with a loan that we can say this. But with a deposit, a person will certainly be brazen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies רבה's reasoning to answer 'what is different about a loan?' The embarrassment logic only exists with a loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower is embarrassed because the lender did him a favor. The owner of a deposit did the שומר no favor, so the שומר has no reason to hold back from a full lie. That is why the partial-admission logic is tied to a מלוה and not a פקדון.

keyTerms.meaning: A deposit: an item left with someone to guard

steps.whatToRemember: The oath for מודה במקצת rests on the חזקה that a borrower won't brazenly lie to his lender, who did him a favor. That reasoning fits a מלוה. With a פקדון, a person will lie to the owner's face (מעיז ומעיז).
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as saying a שומר who denies a deposit is believed without an oath. The point is the opposite: a שומר is not given the 'too embarrassed to lie' trust at all.

phrases.aramaic: וְגַבֵּי מִלְוָה הוּא דְּאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי,
phrases.english: And it is with a loan that this can be said,
but with a deposit, he will certainly act brazenly.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְגַבֵּי מִלְוָה הוּא דְּאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבה's reasoning from steps 3 and 4 to answer the question of step 2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The partial-admission logic belongs to a loan because of the borrower's embarrassment before his lender. With a deposit there is no such embarrassment (מעיז ומעיז), so a שומר who denies the whole deposit is not trusted any more than one who admits part. He too must swear.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא begins a teaching about the four guardians
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא starts quoting a ברייתא about the four kinds of שומרים. The ruling itself is not stated yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא taught a ברייתא: the four kinds of guardians...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It starts quoting a ברייתא from רמי בר חמא about the four kinds of guardians, but the ruling itself comes in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the discussion said that the special partial-admission logic belongs to a loan, not to a deposit. Now a new source is brought in that talks about all four guardians, and guardians are people who hold deposits. So the learner should watch how this ברייתא fits with what was just said about deposits.

keyTerms.meaning: taught. Used when a sage recites a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself.
an אמורא, the sage who recites this ברייתא
the four kinds of guardians: unpaid guardian, paid guardian, renter, and borrower
a guardian, someone who holds another person's property

steps.confusionAlert: Don't stop reading here thinking you know the ruling. The sentence is unfinished, and what the ברייתא says about the four guardians comes right after.

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama teaches:
phrases.notes: תָּנֵי means he is reciting a ברייתא, not giving his own opinion.

phrases.english: The four types of guardians
phrases.notes: These are the unpaid guardian, the paid guardian, the renter and the borrower.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 5 limited the partial-admission logic to a loan, this step brings in a ברייתא about guardians, who hold deposits. It opens a new line that the next text will develop.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not yet stated. Only the opening words, the four kinds of guardians, appear here, and the ruling follows in the next text.
